A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AutoElicit study. All 29 pages of v4 and 32 pages of v5, including appendices, are available and readable. Equations, tables and figures can be matched across revisions and relocation.

before.justification: V4 reports original experiments on synthetic and clinical datasets, including predictive performance, expert-guided elicitation, dataset memorisation and in-context learning analyses.

after.justification: V5 retains these original experiments and adds alternative-prior comparisons and component-count sensitivity results in Figures 12, 13 and 17.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-mixture elicitation procedure, expert-text supplementation, MLE extraction of in-context parameter distributions and Bayes-factor selection remain unchanged. The added comparisons and component-count experiments test the existing method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic linear task and UTI, Heart Disease, Hypothyroid, Diabetes and Breast Cancer datasets. New experiments reuse this coverage. Additional UTI recruitment documentation does not establish a changed population or dataset.

E2.justification: V4 discusses Gouk and Gao (2024) without evaluating their approach. V5 adds their generated-data baseline with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4-turbo, including a regression adaptation. Figure 12 also adds a random-mean, 100-component uninformative mixture comparator against GPT-3.5-turbo and DeepSeek AutoElicit. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: New experiments evaluate 16, 36, 64 and 100 mixture components and introduce a control with 100 standard-normal component means and unit component variances (A.9.4 and A.12). Existing experiments retain their splits, preprocessing, metrics and sampling budgets.

E4.justification: V5 adds substantive controls testing whether mixture complexity explains AutoElicit's gains and whether component count affects posterior predictive performance. The latter covers two LLMs across all six tasks (Figure 17), extending v4's component-count analysis beyond distances between prior distributions. Existing expert-information and memorisation analyses remain.

E5.justification: The existing repeated-split, confidence-interval and mean/standard-deviation reporting remains unchanged. New plots report ten repeats, extending the established practice; no increased run count for retained experiments, new seed policy or new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Figures 12, 13 and 17 add substantial comparative and sensitivity results. AutoElicit beats the generated-data baseline on synthetic and UTI tasks, while baseline advantages include Heart Disease with GPT-4-turbo and Diabetes with GPT-3.5-turbo. Component-count effects are generally small, with a Breast Cancer/DeepSeek exception. Figure 3 also changes reported medians from 0.40 to 0.39 and 0.43 to 0.42.

T1.justification: V5 removes v4 Equation 3, the explicit AutoElicit posterior-predictive formulation, and its accompanying explanation in Section 4.1. The MLE derivation, energy-statistic definition and Bayes-factor formulation remain unchanged apart from numbering.

C1.justification: The abstract and main contribution statements retain the same claims: informative LLM-elicited priors, natural-language expert supplementation, comparison with in-context learning, model selection and reduced UTI labelling requirements. The conclusion retains the same substantive scope.

C2.justification: V5 adds feature-level interpretability discussion in A.13 and explanations for why component count can change prior density more than predictive performance in A.12. A.9.5 hypothesises that memorisation explains some generated-data baseline successes. These are interpretive additions; the main limitations section is substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: A.1 adds a separate AutoElicit repository link for applying the method to new datasets. A.7.1 adds UTI recruitment and consent details. Figure 7 newly discloses a single-Gaussian assumption for the regression calculations; its plotted results are unchanged, so this does not establish a procedural revision.

R1.justification: V5 expands related work on automated model discovery, perception/action priors and Bayesian interpretations of in-context learning, including Li, Wang and Falck papers, and adds Hollmann et al. (2025). It sharpens distinctions from Selby and Gouk and Gao. Publication updates to existing references are not additional works.

P1.justification: V5 applies copyediting, standardises heading capitalisation, corrects cross-references and adds an impact statement and several appendix subsections. Some paragraphs are expanded or shortened, but the principal narrative and section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V5 adds Figures 12, 13 and 17, enlarges and redraws Figure 3 with revised axes and labels, updates captions and relocates tables and appendix figures. The other 17 existing figure graphics are retained, with renumbering where needed; the overall visual format remains similar.

improvement.justification: V5 strengthens the unchanged method's empirical support through a relevant competing approach, a mixture-complexity control and sensitivity tests of actual predictive performance. Additional code access and study documentation improve transparency. These are useful but bounded gains: implementation details for the new generated-data baseline remain limited, and its proposed memorisation explanation is not directly demonstrated.
